Peter,
We are coming up on my favorite event of the year: the Golden Tennis Shoe Awards.
You see, I never planned to take part in politics. But when the state threatened to shut down my kids’ preschool program, I drove to Olympia to fight for it. And while I was there, a male legislator told me that I couldn’t make a difference because I was “just a mom in tennis shoes.” I got angry, but I also got into action. There was no way I was going to let that stop me from fighting for my community and going on to serve as the first woman – and first mom – representing Washington state in the U.S. Senate.
That’s why each year at the Golden Tennis Shoe Awards, I recognize a few people from Washington state who stood up despite the odds and overcame big obstacles to make a difference in their communities.
**[**Do you know a hero in your community who deserves to be recognized for their work at the Golden Tennis Shoe Awards this year? Nominate them now.**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/137850172/642152330/-1685103362?email=dpwillis67@gmail.com&zip=18326&ask=5&amounts=5,25,50,100,250&code=jtk717-fr-nd&refcode=jtk717-fr-nd&recurring=0&sustainers=0&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMzAvMS85MDM4NCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICI3MjMyODdlZS0xN2EwLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=GMBuQA45_JhEMU_oux5_G19mWh_nAPzFcu-Ydfq_fH4=&emci=b9d402a3-df9f-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&emdi=723287ee-17a0-f111-9b33-0022482a9f1d&ceid=13116610)**
**If you know someone from Washington state who has gone above and beyond to create a positive change in their community, I want to hear their story, so I can recognize their dedication to fighting for what they believe in.**

Stats like this from California are the canary in the coal mine, Team. Kern County went from 332 uncounted, late ballots in 2024 to 3,303 in 2025. 📅 **August 24th Update** 🗳️ **Noteworthy Events** Last Tuesday, I attended an “issues” policy briefing focused on likely general‐election voters.On Wednesday morning, I met with GOP Congressional candidate Jay Feely, who is running to replace Congressman David Schweikert in District 1. Later that day, I joined a Colorado River water update hosted by the Central Arizona Project (CAP). CAP and the Arizona Department of Water Resources continue working with water users across the Lower Basin states—Arizona, California, and Nevada—as well as the federal government, on a two‐year agreement designed to provide stability for CAP users and the entire Colorado River system.
On Saturday morning, I joined Jay Feely along with other elected officials for the grand opening of his campaign headquarters in Scottsdale.💧 **Arizona Water Update** Late last week, the federal government finalized a two‐year emergency plan to protect the Colorado River system. The plan imposes deep water cuts on Lower Basin states while sparing Upper Basin states (Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, New Mexico) from mandatory reductions.The Colorado River supplies water to 40 million people across seven states, and federal officials say the action was necessary after years of drought, shrinking reservoirs, and stalled negotiations.📉 What This Means for ArizonaArizona will face major water reductions in 2027 and 2028, with the possibility of even deeper cuts after 2028 if conditions worsen. These reductions affect:
* 🏙️ cities and towns
* 🚜 agriculture and food production
* 🪶 tribal communities
* 📈 long‐term water planning and conservation efforts

The federal plan places a disproportionate burden on Arizona, as Upper Basin states will not share in mandatory reductions. These future cuts pose a serious threat to our state’s long‐term water security.⚠️ Why the Federal Government Stepped InDisagreements between the Upper and Lower Basin states prevented a seven‐state consensus. With key river‐management agreements expiring at the end of 2026—and reservoir levels at historic lows—the federal government intervened to prevent:
* ⚡ hydropower shutdowns
* 🏗️ infrastructure breakdowns
* 📉 further declines in Lake Mead and Lake Powell

The new plan serves as a bridge until a long‐term post‐2026 operating framework can be negotiated.🔭 What Comes NextNow that the 2027–2028 cuts are set, the seven states must negotiate a new long‐term management plan for the river. Discussions continue regarding the imbalance in reductions and whether Arizona will pursue legal action in response to the federal decision.🗳️ **What’s on Your November Ballot?** There are 71 days until the November election. Early ballots will be mailed on October 7th. body:
| | | Hi Peter, Today was another landmark day in what’s turning out to be an epic battle over mail-in voting. If you’re following along, this is the Trump Executive Order / USPS saga where the federal government wants to insert postal workers between you and your ballot. Today, **the Supreme Court lifted one of two court orders** that Colorado and many other states had won in federal court back in June. These orders block harmful new postal rules from taking effect. We had two. Now we have one. But most importantly, **nothing changes for mail ballots right now.** However, USPS is ready to launch its new rules and last Friday night (very late, because they thought we wouldn’t notice?) they published the details. **It would require election officials to provide voter data to the post office.** It would require all ballot envelopes to be pre-scanned and verified before they could be mailed. It would give them the power to reject ballots for mailing. **That’s objectively a terrible idea,** so what’s next? Fortunately, **the Supreme Court did not rule that Trump’s executive order is constitutional or that the USPS rule is legal.** The Court basically said Colorado and the other states sued too early, before USPS had finalized its rule and before anyone was negatively impacted. Well, now the rule is final. The legal arguments all change, so you can be sure this fight is not over. For now, the second court order still prevents USPS from implementing these changes for November. But **I don’t want to downplay how serious this is** , and how significant an impact it could have on our elections. Election officials could be forced to make major changes to mail voting on an extremely short timeline. I am very concerned. **I'm concerned, but not complacent.** I'm reading the rulings, collaborating with others across Colorado and around the country. I’m planning for what we’ll need to do if the election landscape shifts again. **I’ll keep you updated** the next time somebody in Washington decides ballots should only be delivered during a full moon by certified carrier pigeon, or whatever big idea comes next. **We can’t get complacent about this race, either.** Colorado’s next Secretary of State will be responsible for protecting our elections through the rest of this administration and preparing us for 2028. subject: A major decision from the Supreme Court on mail-in voting
disclaimer_text: Paid for by Swing Left, [swingleft
body:
This could have major impacts on military members, overseas citizens, the elderly, recently naturalized citizens, and voters with disabilities who rely on mail voting.
#
Hi there,
Tomorrow marks 10 weeks until Election Day, and today the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) issued a decision that could allow the Trump administration to push through an Executive Order restricting mail-in voting.
This comes after Trump, who claims that vote-by-mail cost him the election in 2020, issued the Executive Order back in March. The order requires that the Postal Service only deliver ballots to individuals on a state-specific list—voters not on this list would be restricted from mail-in voting.
This could have major impacts on voters, including military members, overseas citizens, the elderly, recently naturalized citizens, and voters with disabilities who rely on mail voting.
As always, the Trump administration is looking to make it harder for Americans to vote, because they know Republicans are in danger of losing the House and the Senate this November.
**What you need to know: This isn’t the end of the road for mail-in voting. Today’s ruling changes nothing for voters. The states—not Trump or the USPS—still run our elections.** SCOTUS ruled on a technicality, not the legality of the order. Again, nothing changes for voters right now. There is still a nationwide court order preventing implementation of this Executive Order, and there are potentially more legal challenges, too. We’ll continue to update you as we learn more.
**In the meantime, this SCOTUS ruling won’t change anything we do at Swing Left. It just makes our work to win races in swing districts and states even more important, so that Democrats can win majorities by margins too large for Trump to contest by false mail-in voting claims or otherwise.**
Trump won’t stop, so neither can we. The most impactful thing we can do right now is support candidates and volunteers who talk to voters in competitive races, so we can net enough votes that these efforts by the Supreme Court and the Trump administration won’t have an impact this November.
If Trump’s order ultimately moves forward, campaigns and candidates will need the resources to adapt quickly, as they’ll need to invest in more ads and larger field programs to contact voters about the changes to mail-in voting.
[**If you’d like to arm Democrats with the financial power to weather changes to their races and keep reaching voters, give now to Swing Left’s Balance of Power Fund.**](https://act.swingleft.org/go/27?c0=sl-balance-of-power-2026.KwVigu&refcode=em20260824-2561&t=1&akid=2561%2E1562180%2EGfA7jF)

This fund supports the Democrats running in the most important House and Senate races that will determine control of Congress next year, in addition to supporting Swing Left as we work to organize in competitive states and districts across the country.
Thank you, as always, for your support.
— The Swing Left Team

**Since 2017, Swing Left has channeled the energy of grassroots volunteers and donors to elect Democrats, up and down the ballot, focusing on the most competitive races that can swing the national balance of power.** Right now, Swing Left is investing in grassroots organizing in key swing districts and initiatives across the country to flip the House and win the Senate and critical states in 2026. clean_body: This could have major impacts on military members, overseas citizens, the elderly, recently naturalized citizens, and voters with disabilities who rely on mail voting. Hi there, Tomorrow marks 10 weeks until Election Day, and today the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) issued a decision that could allow the Trump administration to push through an Executive Order restricting mail-in voting. This comes after Trump, who claims that vote-by-mail cost him the election in 2020, issued the Executive Order back in March. The order requires that the Postal Service only deliver ballots to individuals on a state-specific list—voters not on this list would be restricted from mail-in voting. This could have major impacts on voters, including military members, overseas citizens, the elderly, recently naturalized citizens, and voters with disabilities who rely on mail voting. As always, the Trump administration is looking to make it harder for Americans to vote, because they know Republicans are in danger of losing the House and the Senate this November. What you need to know: This isn’t the end of the road for mail-in voting. Today’s ruling changes nothing for voters. The states—not Trump or the USPS—still run our elections. SCOTUS ruled on a technicality, not the legality of the order. Again, nothing changes for voters right now. There is still a nationwide court order preventing implementation of this Executive Order, and there are potentially more legal challenges, too. We’ll continue to update you as we learn more. In the meantime, this SCOTUS ruling won’t change anything we do at Swing Left. It just makes our work to win races in swing districts and states even more important, so that Democrats can win majorities by margins too large for Trump to contest by false mail-in voting claims or otherwise. Trump won’t stop, so neither can we. The most impactful thing we can do right now is support candidates and volunteers who talk to voters in competitive races, so we can net enough votes that these efforts by the Supreme Court and the Trump administration won’t have an impact this November. If Trump’s order ultimately moves forward, campaigns and candidates will need the resources to adapt quickly, as they’ll need to invest in more ads and larger field programs to contact voters about the changes to mail-in voting. This fund supports the Democrats running in the most important House and Senate races that will determine control of Congress next year, in addition to supporting Swing Left as we work to organize in competitive states and districts across the country. Thank you, as always, for your support. — The Swing Left Team Since 2017, Swing Left has channeled the energy of grassroots volunteers and donors to elect Democrats, up and down the ballot, focusing on the most competitive races that can swing the national balance of power. body:
Why October money won't help me| | | | [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/137851376/642196036/724950626?refcode=260824-oct-money-rs&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMzMvMS85NTkyOCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjMTZiZmZmMi0yM2EwLWYxMTEtOWIzMy0wMDIyNDgyYTlmMWQiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=AdxVoaNa6WL8rqfkpDro0NJM6cwrkG524ck82YD0Y-U=)
---
I want to explain how campaigns actually work, because it matters far more than most of the fundraising deadlines you hear about. Television time gets bought months in advance. The main House Republican super PAC booked its fall advertising back in the spring. They reserved $153 million worth of ads across the country, the biggest initial reservation in the group's history. Nearly $7 million of that is already reserved against me here in Southwest Washington. And that's just one Republican group. Donald Trump's MAGA Inc. is sitting on more than $400 million. Elon Musk has authorized at least $100 million in spending to help Republicans this fall. These aren't numbers someone made up for a fundraising email. This is money that already exists. And Republicans know exactly which races they need to win. **And I’m at the top of their list. **So when millions of dollars in attacks start running against me this fall, we can't wait until then to figure out how we'll respond. The money to answer them needs to already be sitting in our account. I know this is not the most exciting email I could send you. name: James Carville
subject: Stopped me cold...
body:
It’s
Carville.

UVA's Center for Politics — one of the most respected election forecasters
in the country — updated its race ratings, and now New Hampshire is listed
as the most competitive Democratic-held seat in the country.

They see what we see — one-point polls, an onslaught of outside spending
attacking Chris, and a candidate from a political dynasty with statewide
name ID.

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260824_3.9DxGn9&refcode=em20260824-3&t=1001&akid=8500%2E582294%2EGC3ZTA ]🚨 Rush a contribution to Chris Pappas right now. New Hampshire just
became the Senate race that needs your attention most.

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260824_3.9DxGn9&amount=5&refcode=em20260824-3&t=1020&akid=8500%2E582294%2EGC3ZTA ]Donate $5 »

Let me tell you what this rating change means in plain English. The
forecasters are telling us that Chris Pappas in New Hampshire – a state
Kamala Harris narrowly won – is now on shakier ground than any other
Democrat running in a currently blue Senate seat.

Why? Because John Sununu — yeah, those Sununus — is a uniquely dangerous
opponent. He's got the famous last name and a Republican machine that has
over $25 million in TV reservations and Koch-backed super PACs already on
the air. He's the kind of candidate that can win in a purple state like
New Hampshire if we don’t treat him like the threat he is.

The forecasters see how close this race is.

The GOP sees what a huge opportunity they have.

I need you to see that this is the most important Senate race in the
country for you to pay attention to right now.

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260824_3.9DxGn9&amount=5&refcode=em20260824-3&t=1039&akid=8500%2E582294%2EGC3ZTA ]Donate $5 »

Here's what I keep coming back to: The ratings are shifting in Democrats’
direction in other Senate races across the country, but our chances in New
Hampshire aren’t moving because it’s not getting the same level of
attention.

That’s why I am telling you this: Right now, dollar for dollar, Chris
Pappas is where your investment in a Democratic Senate majority matters
most.

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260824_3.9DxGn9&refcode=em20260824-3&t=1040&akid=8500%2E582294%2EGC3ZTA ]Rush a contribution to Chris Pappas today. $10, $25, whatever you can
spare. Because if we keep treating New Hampshire like it's someone else's
problem, we're going to wake up in November one seat short of a majority.

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260824_3.9DxGn9&amount=5&refcode=em20260824-3&t=1059&akid=8500%2E582294%2EGC3ZTA ]Donate $5 »

I've been warning about New Hampshire for months. The forecasters just
caught up. Now I need you to step up for Chris right now.

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260824_3.9DxGn9&refcode=em20260824-3&t=1060&akid=8500%2E582294%2EGC3ZTA ]Give what you can right now. Let's win this damn thing and flip
control of the Senate.

— James Carville

[ https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260824_3.9DxGn9&refcode=em20260824-3&t=1061&akid=8500%2E582294%2EGC3ZTA ]James Carville

You can unsubscribe from this mailing list at any time:

| | | | | | Hello Peter,

Tomorrow, I’d love to see you in West Chester!Please join us for **From Conversation to Congress: A Meet & Greet Reception** — an opportunity to come together, talk about the issues affecting our communities, and discuss the kind of leadership we need in Washington.

### FROM CONVERSATION TO CONGRESS
###
**Meet & Greet Reception with Dr. Vanessa Enoch**📅 **Tuesday, August 25, 2026**
⏰ **6:30 PM – 8:00 PM**
📍 **Hummus & Pita**
7334 Tylers Corner Dr.
West Chester, OH 45069
This campaign is about more than winning an election. It is about listening to people across Ohio’s 8th Congressional District and turning those conversations into **real solutions and real impact**.
I want to hear from you.
What issues are affecting your family? What concerns do you have about our community and our country? What should Congress be doing differently?Come meet me, bring your questions and ideas, and learn more about our vision for building a stronger future for the people of Ohio’s 8th District.

### RSVP TODAY
**RSVP here:**
[ https://campaignhq.app/rsvp/hummusandpita](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=141e20202c&e=c6e7dff14c)
And please bring a friend, neighbor, colleague, or family member. The more people we bring into the conversation, the stronger our movement becomes.
**Your Voice. Your District. Your Campaign.**
I hope to see you tomorrow evening!
**Dr. Vanessa Enoch**
Democratic Nominee for U.S. Congress
Ohio’s 8th Congressional District
[https://enochforcongress.com](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=4460636033&e=c6e7dff14c)
**Donate:** [https://enochforcongress.com/donate-now](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=3faa64af2a&e=c6e7dff14c)
**Volunteer:** [https://campaignhq.app](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=fabb2c8921&e=c6e7dff14c)
_Paid for by Committee to Elect Enoch, Catherine Johnson, Treasurer._
* * *

[](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=2ef0223887&e=c6e7dff14c)
# YARD SIGNS ARE GONE!

WE NEED YOUR HELP TO REPLENISH THEM!!!

### GET ON THE WAITING LIST TO GET A YARD SIGN BELOW:

[https://enochforcongress.com/product/free-yard-sign/](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=76ca914060&e=c6e7dff14c)
After you request yours, encourage a neighbor, friend or family member in the district to request one too.
**Let's make support for this campaign visible throughout OH-8.**
* * *

# COME MEET DR. ENOCH
We also have several opportunities coming up to meet Dr. Vanessa Enoch, talk about the issues, and get involved in the campaign.[****](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=da18c409ab&e=c6e7dff14c)
## MEET THE CANDIDATE
### Major Minor Books and Such
**Thursday, August 27**
**7:00 PM – 8:30 PM**
_Doors open at 6:45 PM_**Major Minor Books and Such**
6718 Montgomery Rd.
Cincinnati, OH 45236
Come meet Dr. Enoch and hear about her priorities for Ohio's 8th Congressional District, including protecting Social Security and Medicare, lowering healthcare and prescription drug costs, strengthening veterans' services, creating jobs, expanding affordable housing, investing in American manufacturing, and holding government accountable.
Bring your questions — and bring a friend. [RSVP here](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=8a148533e2&e=c6e7dff14c).
* * *
[](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=b39440c437&e=c6e7dff14c)
## CANVASS GREENHILLS WITH US!
### Canvass for Jonathan Bradner & Dr. Vanessa Enoch
**Sunday, August 30**
**2:00 PM – 5:00 PM****Drummond St. & Damon Rd.**
99 Drummond Street
Greenhills, Ohio
The Cincinnati Working Families Party Wolf Pack is organizing a [canvass covering **Greenhills A, B and C. RSVP on Mobilize here.**](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=1d3b3a4bbf&e=c6e7dff14c)
No canvassing experience is necessary. **Training will be provided.**
Bring a fully charged phone, comfortable walking shoes, and a friend.
* * *
# WE HAVE A LOT OF WORK TO DO — AND NOT A LOT OF TIME.
This campaign is growing.People are volunteering.People are requesting signs.People are attending events.People are knocking doors.And voters are beginning to hear our message.
**Now we need to scale.**
That requires resources.When you contribute to this campaign, you aren't simply making a donation. **You're helping us communicate with voters who may otherwise never hear about this race.**
You're helping us put up the signs.You're helping us run the ads.You're helping us print the literature.You're helping us knock the doors.You're helping us build the field operation.And ultimately, **you're helping give voters in Ohio's 8th Congressional District a real choice.**

### Please make a contribution today.

**DONATE:**
[ https://enochforcongress.com/donate-now/](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=5659e303ff&e=c6e7dff14c)
**REQUEST A YARD SIGN:**
[ https://enochforcongress.com/product/free-yard-sign/](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=c3867f7635&e=c6e7dff14c)
**VOLUNTEER:**
[ https://campaignhq.app](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=3fae20fdd1&e=c6e7dff14c)
[Whether you can give **$10, $25, $50, $100, $250 or more** , your contribution moves us closer to the resources we need to compete.](https://enochforcongress.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=488c703b71891f0b712737c99&id=0e8592ad42&e=c6e7dff14c)
**We can do this — but we have to do it together.** Thank you for believing in this campaign and in what we are working to build for Ohio's 8th Congressional District.
**Dr. Vanessa Enoch**
Democratic Nominee for Congress
Ohio's 8th Congressional District
**Enough of Excuses. It's Time for Results.****Real Leadership. Real Solutions. A Stronger Ohio.**

name: Mary Peltola
subject: I’m officially running in the general election for U.S. Senate in Alaska
disclaimer_text: Paid for by VPP
body:
| Hello -

My name is Mary Peltola, and after winning last week's primary, I am officially running in the general election for United States Senate in Alaska.

I want to share with you why I made the decision to run – and to ask for your support as we begin the general election together.

But if you already understand how important this race and your support are, and you’re ready to join our fight for fish, family, and freedom, please use this button to split a contribution between my campaign for U.S. Senate and the Voter Protection Project: | [CONTRIBUTE »](https://act.protectvoting.org/go/126285?t=6&akid=28068%2E878179%2Ej-YhMw)
---
Now here’s a bit more on how I came to this decision.

When I was growing up in Bethel, salmon fishing with my father in the summers and dog mushing in the winters, Alaska was a place of abundance.

Now, all across Alaska, we have scarcity.

Multi-national companies are trawling our waters and decimating our fish stocks. The moose, caribou, and migratory birds that used to fill our freezers are harder to find.

So we buy more groceries, where the prices are just crushing Alaska families.

And I've got to tell you, DC people do not care that we are paying nearly 20 bucks for a gallon of fuel. They don’t even believe us.

They're focused on their own wallets – not ours.

And when they actually work together on something, it’s usually to help themselves. The rigged system in DC is shutting down Alaska and hurting all of us while politicians and their millionaire and billionaire donors feather their own nest.

It’s why our prices keep rising, all while the healthcare and services Alaskans rely on get gutted.

I'm done with politicians getting richer while things get tougher here at home.

My agenda for Alaska will always be: fish, family, freedom. These values have been the core values of my campaigns since the very beginning.

But if we’re going to secure Alaska’s future, we need another priority: fighting corruption.

I'm running for Alaska's Senate seat because it is the fight for our future.

**This is going to be the closest and most consequential Senate race this year, and I cannot do this alone. There is only one way we’ll be able to flip this seat... and that is together.**

So I am asking:

[Please split a contribution between the Voter Protection Project and my campaign for the U.S. Senate today as we begin the general election. We are looking for a huge number of day one donors to get our general election campaign off to a strong start and put us in a position to win. No donation is too small. They will all add up fast to give us the resources we need to WIN in November. ](https://act.protectvoting.org/go/126285?t=7&akid=28068%2E878179%2Ej-YhMw)
If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your split donation between Mary Peltola and VPP will go through immediately:

Thank you,

Mary

name: Sam Williams
subject: Molder For Congress - Moms For Molder Launch This Saturday!
body:
Good Morning Y'all,
We’re excited to officially launch **Moms for Molder** this Saturday, August 29, at Pinkerton Park in Franklin!
Moms for Molder is about bringing together moms who want a representative in Washington who is focused on making it easier to raise a family in Tennessee. Chaz will talk about his plans to lower costs, support strong schools and make sure working families can get ahead, and he wants to hear directly from moms about what their families need from Congress.

We’ll have kid-friendly food, _special Moms for Molder campaign merchandise_ and a playground nearby, so there’s no need to find a sitter.
**Moms for Molder Launch**
**Date:** Saturday, August 29
**Time:** 12:00 to 1:00 p.m.
**Location:** Pinkerton Park in Franklin
RSVP to [sam@chazmolder.com](mailto:sam@chazmolder.com) for the exact meeting spot.
Bring the kids, invite another mom and come be part of the launch. We hope to see you there!

\- Team Molder

## Supreme Court OKs Trump Mail-in Vote Restrictions
The Supreme Court on Monday [cleared the way](https://email.editor.jointheflyover.com/c/eJykkL-upSAQxp8GOwyOipyCYhu7s-2WBmE4skExMGr27Tfc-wi3m2S-P_l9f97L24QYjs9vs6Mmn5YDnxKRCPOymxDvROH4ZCyUg6WQjlLQLiBAcqE4jIuxFG5cBtM47REB-wZ1N6lJjgBCNptWHmzXv1blp26VMK5KDMaj8s6rTvqhCbrmCQVjJ0QPsnVgXqg6HCYzrasa2SDQBUq5_ZvCQRv6-C_dmFub9ibqjegsrP_FYGYwP8_T2rVUjvpnMNeTwVyuM-OO3KYrE6d87SeviPybkafsMPOrnIW7rRqarN35hBhDkRMbxKeqvzrph1PdGv4HAAD__zGugO8) for President Trump to move ahead with his executive order restricting mail-in voting before November's midterms. The three liberal justices dissented from the unsigned order. The March order, which Trump casts as a safeguard against fraud and noncitizen voting, directs the government to build lists of eligible voters and bars the U.S. Postal Service from delivering mail ballots to anyone not on them. ## Postal Carriers Charged in Check Scheme
Three Houston mail carriers are among five people [federally charged](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkLHO3CAQhJ8Gd5xgjW1cUKRx96dNaa1hfaBgc4L9fZe3j5xXSDUazWg0-n59rV-YcjqfP_Egx5-9rCe9WyZmqmsk5DdedBLWVsmXGhp-N04rKBilshKGFT2ni1aDXXCbCrPuyOnJTuMwjLbvoqOAVo27RwMbokWjMAy7N4P1GMw8dcndc8rCoLXSen4M80zzqLG3ysK2WWEUhcSlPjgS0wfbnv-Ui-rDl6PLLjK_muh_CFgELLh53d-JgOVVGgtYYvluXE55W8zSY62JapM-Yn1SkJgz3Qq9PFLOqZzSR_K_JUfaWTYf6SABi54nML0aBSxddeH1vsttnIRRzwNT_veH_5fj5eBvAAAA__-0D4kS) in a scheme prosecutors say moved nearly $24 million in checks stolen from the mail. A federal grand jury [indicted](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkD2y4yAMx0-DO2WwYju4oNjG3dt2S48MSmCCTQaU8Pb2O94rvE7FT_-vP1_rF8UUj8dv2tnK9z2vB7eaWITLGpik0YcPplILu1x8pXeVuKLGCbQBHFdyEj-8DtR5u2k_9x3b_mZu0zhO5toF68mgHyZDZMxw4_tkNjRuuA5u85rRddGectrg2Pe67-fLOM88Tz1djTa4bUYNmn2UXC4SWPib6j39zR8uF5f3Ltkg8qrq-kvhonBprV1ciu6JIb-r5OOkFC5nMYVLyo6SwuX0VLhoc97D-RdIoDE8j9yAtvwWkMAwwovzKzG4QOXBHuIBBPs7SYQ9phTzAT6nRAVcYPeE6gLvrHDpivWvdiJ1uqlBP3aK6X9k-enUH4v_AgAA___pDZSO) Tryston Vaughn, Catherine Kilpatrick, Drakkor Alexander, Malcolm Joubert, and Alyssa Bryant on Aug. 19. Prosecutors say Vaughn recruited Kilpatrick, Alexander, and Joubert to pull checks off their delivery routes, then resold them. The checks were posted for sale on a [Telegram channel](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkDGO5CAURE-DM1rwMTYOCDZxNptuaGH4DGiwGcHvdu_tV94rTFgqqVTv_fnYPlwu-fz87Q609I51O_HqBYmwbQkdXe6FJ7rWG_raQnfPTnkDARMXhoPenKf8wm10Q7C7CIsc0MrZzJPWk1FDsmDEqGESEqWKMnqtJXqYnJ9QzVqrIdt7ThjQUgopl4deFlwm6ZQRBvbdsFFgyFTbgxISvl2P5W99YXv4egzFJqLvztQvBiuD9bqux1eqz7tksLpG2RdksN5kDFbf8nHHVJ-d6sl9Qv_FKWEk3n3CA3k-Q_Z04EkMVjCax0X7uAfNYRkjHxc1cqOU50KIOQTtQew4NBu-r1xK7tPMRvF5uFz-P6Sfmn1Z-BcAAP__0wiL5A) called "slipsandchips" and shipped to buyers through FedEx. They ran from a few thousand dollars up to a $1,517,875.27 check that Joubert allegedly lifted from a Houston route in May 2024. The conspiracy began around October 2022 and targeted accounts at Chase, Amegy, Citibank, BMO, and Stellar Bank, according to the indictment.
## CeeDee Lamb's Home Burglarized
Someone climbed through a side window at Cowboys receiver CeeDee Lamb's Fairview home and walked out with [more than $300,000](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkMGupCAURL9Gdxi4iuKCxWzc9WxnaS5wbcmgGKC1e75-4sv7g7c7SSWVqvPnMT_QB78_f-NGuryXOO905UClUJpXwnLhSTthyolsTC7jKxc_A4eeccVAzmiLP2nusHbacDeKmrQY1NBL2au2XjXCsAwojALqCEbs-CCktHIxZDtFfe31XccVSCG4EGMjx5HGXmCruAJjVNVxcr7E1JSVCr0xL-ETT0qNjVsd9FrKkav2VwVTBdN1Xc1u7P3jziuYbqxgemX2TZbIEbGAm8lsjRsx80rPgMn_I8dazv-yI8WDUvmwZHeUY8dhqJN2x-VD8Lkfqo4_N_Tha0L5qbpTw_8AAAD__4hnhOo) worth of his belongings. People representing him met officers at the door and pointed out the broken window. Investigators believe [a single suspect](https://email.editor.thetexasflyover.com/c/eJykkM2OpCAUhZ8Gdxi8iuKCxaQ7rLprM4tZmqtcSxIsDFBSNU8_cV6hdyc5yXd-_nxP3-i8e9xvuJPOrzVMDyrJU84Up40wFzzpQRhTpCVEm_CZsptAQM-F4iAnXLI7aeqwsnoWdmwq0s2ghl7KXrXVphe7yn62ogfVrqCsICGGVXTSDgok2crpCycUyKYRTTPWchxp7BtslVAwz4p1gqzLIdZ5o0wvTKt_h5NivYS98nrL-Uis_cXAMDCllPp5uMtjYH4fIeY03agkBuZmvhiYK46BEerSLQNzBO8W4lvYiX-i95j4RyhzeCceaSF3UuQfRJ9E_Av3mc_PePcY3V-yDEwrh2uwhE7Ii1ZFbY_ivHepH1gn7js6_79q_unFp4Z_AQAA__9eIo5A) got in and out that way, taking "several high-end personal items." Lamb, 27, is not the first athlete targeted. Eagles running back Saquon Barkley's Pennsylvania home was invaded last month while his family was inside, and three men were indicted last year in a break-in at Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow's home.

We're behind where we should be, even though we've accomplished so much in just over 30 days. Just over four weeks ago, I officially got into this race. I am not a politician - and I think that's a good thing. My opponent has had 20 years to build up his campaign war chest. I have not. What I do have is almost thirty years of working for the people of South Carolina, the values Lindsey and I were both raised on, Every dollar we raise between now and when polls close today matters now more than ever. name: Bill Gray
subject: Are you proud to be an American citizen?
body:
If you’re like me, you give thanks to God every day that you live in a country that is free, peaceful, and where citizens have inalienable rights.

This sponsored message from Inside Scoop Politics is on behalf of Hillsdale College
| | | [](https://email.update.insidescooppolitics.org/c/eJyckcFu3CAQQL8G39ZiB4zxwYdKjk_dpE1b5YhYGHtHwoAMTpV-fZVq0w_IceZJ70kzLxdzsRQoro92w5FKMT55Y3d8S0fe0-FruqKNdsOdnI0GOKgT1yfojHWVXtFI2_ixg7NedIPjude96gbZyeY2LnbgV7WI61l56JW-Kuw7LjVfFo3adQ2N7z6uoTsDF3xopehA4bDwvh9wEZ5JfmRvK7YUC3ksLqWcU6BKrrRpX5sw3mrNhYkvDGYGc0F37OjbG4VQvA3Yoj8YzP9nBrN_o7ieHFX6g5GJuTgmJs4VDI8cJHyVl-lpenj4wUAddTMlHbtDJqa8p5LRVYrrHW3o6diYmHCzFO5LZ7dsaY1MTP9K5qN0xylWjJWJ6dvz06_JfO9PLz-fTx-XaPbR598UAhXVM8nXd3Pr0tbUz_7ndYS_AQAA___9UaFg)
---
| | Dear Fellow American, Are you proud to be an American citizen? If you’re like me, you give thanks to God every day that you live in a country that is free, peaceful, and where citizens have inalienable rights. Most people in history can’t say the same thing—in fact, most people in the world can’t say the same thing even today. You don’t have to be a historian to see that the long practice of citizenship in America is unprecedented. It’s one of our nation’s great achievements. But there’s a catch—citizenship requires vigilance and knowledge to maintain. Especially now, when it faces threats from the far-Left and progressive economic policies, illegal immigration, and more. Everyone who wishes to defend freedom in America requires an understanding of the nature and scope of these challenges. As a college, we know that a proper education is the best defense of liberty. And unlike the vast majority of colleges and universities, we must **reach** and **teach** millions of Americans about liberty. And we have to do it without taking ONE PENNY of government funding—not even indirectly in the form of student grants and loans. NOT. ONE. PENNY—to remain proudly independent. This means that your support is critical to our success. With your help, we’ll engage the far-Left on the battlefield of education. With your help, we will defend liberty against dangerous ideologies. And with your help, we will preserve freedom for future generations of American citizens. You can give safely and securely at this link: [https://secured.hillsdale.edu/hillsdale/dying-citizen](https://email.update.insidescooppolitics.org/c/eJyckcFu3CAQQL8G39ZiB4zxwYdKjk_dpE1b5YhYGHtHwoAMTpV-fZVq0w_IceZJ70kzLxdzsRQoro92w5FKMT55Y3d8S0fe0-FruqKNdsOdnI0GOKgT1yfojHWVXtFI2_ixg7NedIPjude96gbZyeY2LnbgV7WI61l56JW-Kuw7LjVfFo3adQ2N7z6uoTsDF3xopehA4bDwvh9wEZ5JfmRvK7YUC3ksLqWcU6BKrrRpX5sw3mrNhYkvDGYGc0F37OjbG4VQvA3Yoj8YzP9nBrN_o7ieHFX6g5GJuTgmJs4VDI8cJHyVl-lpenj4wUAddTMlHbtDJqa8p5LRVYrrHW3o6diYmHCzFO5LZ7dsaY1MTP9K5qN0xylWjJWJ6dvz06_JfO9PLz-fTx-XaPbR598UAhXVM8nXd3Pr0tbUz_7ndYS_AQAA___9UaFg) **And for a gift of $100 or more, you’ll receive a special hardcover edition of Victor Davis Hanson’s book,** **_The Dying Citizen: How Progressive Elites, Tribalism, and Globalization Are Destroying the Idea of America_****. Victor Davis Hanson is a frequent commentator on Fox News and online. He’s also a historian and distinguished fellow here at Hillsdale.** Regarding the book, my boss and teacher, Hillsdale President Larry P. Arnn, has written, “In this book, Hanson demonstrates yet again his command across time and for our time. **This book and he are a treasure.** ” Thank you so much for your partnership in promoting the kind of intelligent patriotism—especially among younger Americans—that is essential to preserving citizenship and free government.
---
| | Warm regards, Bill Gray, ’01
Vice President
National Donor Outreach
Hillsdale College

It was Food Truck Friday in Opelika, and we were handing out cards. Things were going well when a gentleman approached me. I handed him one of my cards and said, "My name is Lee McInnis, and I'm running for Congress in Alabama's 3rd District."
He looked at the card for a minute and asked, "Are you a conservative?"
Since words can mean a lot of things in 2026, I asked what conservative meant to him. "Do you believe in lowering taxes?" he asked.
"Absolutely," I replied, "I believe in lowering taxes on working people and a tax code that taxes everyone fairly."
He nodded. "Okay, do you believe in small government?"
"Again, yes.," I said. "I believe the government should focus on programs that only it can do or that directly benefit the people. I don't believe the government has any place in your bedroom, bathroom, or doctor's office."
"What about the federal debt?" he asked.
"The federal debt reached $40 trillion today. That's ridiculous. We've got to get it under control."
He stared at my card for a really long moment. I couldn't wait for him to figure it out, so I just said, "You know, in 2026, all that makes me a Democrat... right?"
He looked as if he had been betrayed. As if I knew the words to the sacred chants, only to turn out to be a heretic anyway. The consternation on his face was profound. He mumbled something and walked off...

Don't recognize this sender? [Unsubscribe with one click](https://substack..idvc6feHUixiColEw-od4OK6cDjVN1ffy_xV-C5cVkM?)
Congressman Wiley Nickel recently imported your email address from another platform to Substack. You'll now receive their posts via email or the [Substack app](https://substack.com/redirect/a339bb8b-ff5a-4bb3-925e-c1c881817753?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). To set up your profile and discover more on Substack, [click here](https://substack.com/redirect/ec84abad-7390-4f52-8d45-743ce16040f2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/e6035446-0616-42f9-86b8-2370ee3b0a56?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
I want to tell you about a decision I don't regret for a second.
In 2022, I flipped North Carolina's 13th Congressional District from red to blue. It was one of only six Republican seats in the entire country that Democrats won that year. In a brutal cycle, in a purple state, we did it.
Then Republicans in Raleigh took it away without a single vote being cast. They redrew the map and erased my district. The people who elected me were moved into other districts, and the seat I won was gone with them.
I'm not telling you this so you'll feel bad for me. I'm telling you because it's the whole problem in one story.
Gerrymandering is wrecking the US Congress. When politicians get to pick their voters, they draw themselves safe seats where the only threat is a primary from the far right or the far left. So they govern to the extremes. Out of 435 House seats, only around 10% are genuinely competitive anymore. The other 90% are locked up in low-turnout primaries before a single general-election vote is cast, meaning few people in Congress have any real incentive to work across the aisle.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/aed047f3-fe6d-489a-be60-8ca3b50b6458?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
So I didn't just complain about it. I authored the FAIR MAPS Act and introduced it in Congress. It would take map-drawing away from politicians and hand it to independent, nonpartisan redistricting commissions in every state. Duke researchers found a national law like it would double the number of competitive seats in the House. More competition means more accountability, and members who actually have to answer to all their voters.
There's only one way to fix this for good, and it's not complicated. You pass a national law banning partisan gerrymandering. Hakeem Jeffries and House Democrats will pass my bill as soon as they have the votes. I have no doubt about it. The House isn't the problem.
The Senate is the problem. A gerrymandering ban dies in the Senate as long as the filibuster lets a Republican minority block it. The only way it ever becomes law is if Democrats take the Senate, carve out an exception to the filibuster for the fundamental rights that shouldn't hang on a procedural rule -- abortion, voting rights, and an end to partisan gerrymandering -- and then pass the bills.
And the clearest path to flipping the Senate runs through North Carolina.
Which brings me to the decision I want to tell you about.
## **The race I started**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/bf78edab-22f9-461c-86c8-4dbd3e6d03c6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
When Republicans gerrymandered me out of my seat, I could have cashed in. A former congressman can go make a boatload of money lobbying, and plenty do. That's not what I did. I looked at our U.S. Senate seat and thought: that's a fight worth having.
So I started running, and I gave it everything I had. I believe in this state, and I know we've got to fix a broken political system. I lived that. I wasn't going to watch from the sidelines. For a while, I was all in.
## **Then Roy Cooper got in**
I'll be straight with you, because you deserve that. I always believed Roy was the strongest candidate we could put up for this seat. Two-term governor, four-term attorney general, six statewide wins and no losses. He left office more popular than the day he walked in. If you built a candidate in a lab to flip North Carolina blue, you'd build Roy Cooper.
I just never thought he'd run, and I never thought Thom Tillis would step down. When both happened, the math got simple. It wasn't comfortable, but it was pretty easy.
I could have stayed in and made it a primary. Democrats trading punches while Trump takes a wrecking ball to the Constitution. So I got out of the way and endorsed Roy. A united Democratic Party focused on sending Trump a message is how we flip this seat. A bruising primary is how we hand it away. That mattered more to me than staying in the race. It still does.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/4be79650-d806-42ec-822c-ed6bbb6121bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
## **Why Roy, specifically**
Let me tell you what kind of governor Roy Cooper was, because it's the same thing that will make him a great US senator.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/e6035446-0616-42f9-86b8-2370ee3b0a56?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
I was in the North Carolina State Senate from 2019 to 2023. Those were hard years to be a Democrat in that building. We were outnumbered. But we had one job that mattered more than any other: hold the line on Roy's vetoes. And we did. Every single time. Roy vetoed some very bad bills, and Republicans never once overrode him while I was there. Our votes were the firewall between a good governor and a legislature itching to run him over, and that firewall held the whole time.
That's what Roy does to the opposition. They couldn't beat him at the ballot box in six statewide races. For years they couldn't even override his veto and it was good for public policy in our state. Democrats and Republicans had to work together and we're all better off for it.
## **He 's also just a really good guy**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/e6035446-0616-42f9-86b8-2370ee3b0a56?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Roy and I go back. He encouraged me to run for the NC Senate in 2018. Right after I won my seat, he came to Cary and headlined a fundraiser for me. A sitting governor showing up in my hometown for a brand-new state senator. I never forgot it.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/e6035446-0616-42f9-86b8-2370ee3b0a56?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
Adeline approves!
So when people ask why I endorsed him, the head answer is easy. He's the best shot we've had at this seat in forty years. But the gut answer is simpler. He showed up for North Carolina, and I'm going to show up for him. And I don't mean a press release and a retweet. Right after I got out of the race, I hosted a fundraiser for Roy at my home. Endorsing him was never the point. Getting him elected is.
## **Now for the hard truth**

---|---|---
I don't want to oversell this, so I'll give it to you straight.
The good news is real. Roy is running a terrific campaign, and the Cook Political Report recently moved this race from toss-up to lean Democrat, calling it the GOP-held seat Democrats are most likely to flip in the entire country. That's not spin. It's from the most respected race-rating group in the business.
But this is a tough fight. It's always a tough fight in a 50/50 state. Want to know how tough? Since Terry Sanford won in 1986, Democrats have won a U.S. Senate race in North Carolina exactly twice. John Edwards in 1998. Kay Hagan in 2008. Forty years, two wins.
That's the hill we're climbing. Roy Cooper is the best candidate we've had to climb it in a long time. And the other side knows it and they're going to spend an ungodly amount of dark money to try and stop him.

When politicians get to pick their voters, they draw themselves safe seats where the only threat is a primary from the far right or the far left. So they govern to the extremes. Out of 435 House seats, only around 10% are genuinely competitive anymore. The other 90% are locked up in low-turnout primaries before a single general-election vote is cast, meaning few people in Congress have any real incentive to work across the aisle. | | ---|---|--- So I didn't just complain about it. ### Loneliness is an epidemic in America. Policymakers aren't doing enough.
| | [Ben Samuels](https://substack.com/@bensamuels)

It's well understood that loneliness is a crisis in this country. The CDC notes that [1-in-3 Americans feel lonely](https://substack.com/redirect/289efb33-dac3-4478-aade-5fb7dc10965b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg),1 and [article](https://substack.com/redirect/0471fc09-305b-40d7-9d14-4927bf25467b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) [after](https://substack.com/redirect/a5bd6aac-cbb0-46c2-a56f-1da089f89fc0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) [article](https://substack.com/redirect/8cfef6d1-4d8c-4296-8411-aabb80d59c66?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) [after](https://substack.com/redirect/18f543f4-0b9d-40f0-809a-2fa198ba9896?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) [article](https://substack.com/redirect/ad783e8c-a3d9-4a68-8372-604448d5d8fe?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) references the loneliness epidemic in the U.S. and around the world.
By now, everyone seems to get that. The issue is that there isn't one easy fix.
The causes of loneliness are global, but the solutions are manifold, local, disjointed, and often pretty ordinary. Policymakers at every level of government aren't doing enough.
[Subscribed](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9iZW5zYW11ZWxzLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9hY2NvdW50IiwicCI6MjEyMTgzMTkyLCJzIjoyNDQwMzk4LCJmIjp0cnVlLCJ1Ijo5MDUwMTE5MiwiaWF0IjoxNzg3NjY1MDA0LCJleHAiOjIxMDMyNDEwMDQsImlzcyI6InB1Yi0wIiwic3ViIjoibGluay1yZWRpcmVjdCJ9.RiPGVs6r-ZYJfYST2j5722QqDjnCWmAYEMZTSZKDHPg?)
> _**Article summary:**_
> * _Americans, particularly men and younger people, are lonelier than they 've ever been._
> * _Loneliness isn 't just an individual problem. Systemic loneliness means higher mortality rates and lower workforce productivity._
> * _We need policy solutions to chip away at systemic loneliness: addressing social media use, community engagement, and housing are all part of the answer._
>

### The scale of loneliness is staggering
Certainly, people _feel_ lonelier, and both men and women say they have fewer close friends than in the past.
That's especially true among men. In 1990, 55% of men said that they had six or more close friends; in 2021, [that fell to 27%](https://substack.com/redirect/fb36fb2d-6378-458d-96ec-ca00cedb76fb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), at the same time that the percentage of men who said they have no close friends increased by 5×.
The same is true of young people generally: [people ages 18-29 are 4× likelier](https://substack.com/redirect/3590d7ed-ae76-4f98-873e-c204d6fa28ca?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) to say that they're serially lonely relative to people who are 65+. Lower-income Americans [are also much lonelier](https://substack.com/redirect/0e3ba978-8517-4460-9f16-9acb54866a49?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) than wealthier ones.2
But this goes beyond how people are feeling. We can measure clear changes in societal norms and habits too:
* People are far likelier to live alone today than they were 50 years ago. [29% of Americans lived alone in 2024](https://substack.com/redirect/796d9236-57e9-4133-8dcb-1c389a80ebf5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) versus 19% who lived alone in 1974.3
* From 2015 to 2025, the number of people who socialize every day [fell by more than 20%](https://substack.com/redirect/b9396a18-3f02-42af-a63c-b8a08e15e7f6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg),4 and the average time people spend socializing per day dropped at a similar rate.
* 26% of Americans [eat all of their meals alone on any given day](https://substack.com/redirect/e22f31e2-f6af-48d4-8617-c81e02a611bb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), a 50% increase from 2003.
* Even before the COVID-19 pandemic, the [percentage of Americans who regularly spend time with their neighbors](https://substack.com/redirect/461ea054-d74c-4720-8db4-193dff6555ed?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) was in steep decline, having fallen 34% between 1974 and 2018.5

As a society, we're still living in the shadow of the pandemic. I don't know if this is _the_ primary way we're living in that shadow: that may be students having fallen behind in school, or the intense polarization of society that the pandemic exacerbated. But it's clearly one of the durable consequences.
COVID didn't create loneliness; all of the data suggests it had been trending that way for decades. But it very obviously made things worse.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=2440398&post_id=212183192&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjEyMTgzMTkyLCJpYXQiOjE3ODc2NjUwMDQsImV4cCI6MTc5MDI1NzAwNCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTI0NDAzOTgiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.IG2c_mRVLQTkk72SQTX0YmFsSeiERi73vguF-UjkL5g)
### Loneliness is a public health crisis
As I've written before, government's role is to [make people's lives better](https://substack.com/redirect/5dcaa148-4977-4c20-b110-d1ee7f624485?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). If people are serially feeling lonely, it's worth trying to fix that on its own merits.
But this isn't just a question of happiness; the problems run deeper than that.
* **This is a workforce problem**. [Lonely workers miss 5.7 more days per year](https://substack.com/redirect/0b42bf63-af5c-4faa-a22b-f04367792712?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of work than non-lonely workers--more than a full work week. By that estimate, loneliness costs employers $154 billion per year. Loneliness is also associated with [lower job performance, lower job satisfaction, and higher burnout](https://substack.com/redirect/2df6c15f-1200-4391-81b4-d2bb3491bfd3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). On the flip side, people with close social relationships at work [produce better work and stay longer](https://substack.com/redirect/528fadfd-ac79-4aa9-9f04-d0834f87aa29?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).6
* **Loneliness is a health problem**. Serial loneliness and lack of socialization [reduce life expectancies](https://substack.com/redirect/ad539d19-2708-41ff-bf60-9bb135aac014?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). One longitudinal study found that [lonely people live 5.4 fewer years](https://substack.com/redirect/43f44ac2-7d56-45b4-bcbb-978bd07ea306?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) than non-lonely people, which is staggeringly high.7

When people talk about this as a public health emergency, this is why.
### What can policymakers do?
It's not that the U.S. doesn't recognize that this is a problem.8 At the [federal](https://substack.com/redirect/289efb33-dac3-4478-aade-5fb7dc10965b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg),9 state,10 and local levels,11 the government says it's working to address it.
But much of what these government commissions conclude is that more research is needed. Obviously, the data is important, but I don't get the sense that there's enough urgency here given the scale of this problem.
One challenge is that there isn't one simple policy intervention that's going to fix this. Another is that the way people socialize is guided far more by long-evolving norms than by any public policy; you can't (nor should you) pass a law that requires people to hang out with their neighbors.
But that doesn't mean there isn't more we can be doing. Below are examples of policies that would start to address America's loneliness crisis.
#### Limit social media for children
Social media isn't uniformly responsible for loneliness, but it's no accident that just as social media got really big around 2010, the percentage of 12th graders who [spend time with their friends every day](https://substack.com/redirect/64d550b0-afcb-4dea-a303-41e47d07343e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) fell precipitously and loneliness [started sharply rising among adolescents](https://substack.com/redirect/9efe731f-ab81-4109-9b91-1d708ebdc508?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
Social media is here to stay. But elected officials aren't going far enough to protect minors, and teens under 16 shouldn't be allowed to have social media accounts:
[](https://substack.com/redirect/e47dce85-2a05-47d3-a6a8-8bef5f2d543d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)| | |
#### [Ban social media for teens under 16](https://substack.com/redirect/e47dce85-2a05-47d3-a6a8-8bef5f2d543d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

This is a short- and long-term policy solution. Short-term, kids will be less lonely; long-term, they're more likely to develop the skills they need to build and maintain friendships.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=2440398&post_id=212183192&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjEyMTgzMTkyLCJpYXQiOjE3ODc2NjUwMDQsImV4cCI6MTc5MDI1NzAwNCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTI0NDAzOTgiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.IG2c_mRVLQTkk72SQTX0YmFsSeiERi73vguF-UjkL5g)
#### Invest in lasting, recurring community events
More often than not, I'm writing about policy at the federal level or at the state level, usually in Missouri. This policy intervention is at the local level--which is tricky, because local mayors and city councilors wouldn't often include "addressing loneliness" in their mandate.
It should be.
There's data on how team sports increase connectivity and [reduce depression rates for men with mental health issues](https://substack.com/redirect/c00ca92a-18bc-4649-a8b7-cee0b695baf3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). But since 2012, the youth sports participation rate is down, [modestly for girls and significantly for boys](https://substack.com/redirect/24d88cdc-9cae-4723-a1a7-9b59b87502be?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).12
That's a real problem, especially when you consider that back in 2015, [for 45% of teenagers](https://substack.com/redirect/36f6a6a5-d761-4b94-9f30-b4eefb494be7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), team sports and group activities were a big part of how they stayed connected to their closest friends.13
We're moving the wrong way, and I don't think it's an accident that loneliness is climbing as youth sports participation falls.
This doesn't just have to be sports, by the way. Local, affordable, community-based events--team sports or otherwise--empirically help people feel less lonely and make friends. This sort of social infrastructure needs to be seen as a public good.
#### Promote volunteering and service years
I've written before about the importance of volunteering, in part because it [makes people less lonely](https://substack.com/redirect/598bf6a7-fc03-424b-909c-8f0c19856d2f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). But the number of hours that Americans volunteer [is in decline](https://substack.com/redirect/ca6e5ea3-7672-467f-a0bc-6b4d7fb7674d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).14
[](https://substack.com/redirect/d9e5f06e-21fa-423a-8558-83998dd5e84e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)| | |
#### [How to deal with your political angst](https://substack.com/redirect/d9e5f06e-21fa-423a-8558-83998dd5e84e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

Finding [increased opportunities for national service](https://substack.com/redirect/9388eebd-38b2-41ab-93f6-6fbc9093384b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) outside of the military is a start.15 Growing AmeriCorps, which invests in young adults _and_ in the United States, is one such example. These programs help with the transition from high school to adulthood, particularly for people who don't go to four-year college.
These interventions are critical for the so-called [disconnected adults](https://substack.com/redirect/9f8f0057-4780-4c82-b8d9-5aa1673daadb?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), people who are neither employed nor in school. They make up 16% of 18-to-24-year-olds, a huge number when you consider that every year that they aren't working or aren't in school, they become lonelier and much less employable.
We should be growing these programs with disconnected adults in mind specifically.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=2440398&post_id=212183192&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjEyMTgzMTkyLCJpYXQiOjE3ODc2NjUwMDQsImV4cCI6MTc5MDI1NzAwNCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTI0NDAzOTgiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.IG2c_mRVLQTkk72SQTX0YmFsSeiERi73vguF-UjkL5g)
#### Design housing with the goal of addressing loneliness
One of the ideas I find most intriguing: changing the regulations, guidelines, and support for housing with the specific goal of promoting community.
That takes a few forms, which include but aren't limited to:
* Change the design of housing, particularly things like student housing and [senior living facilities](https://substack.com/redirect/d0d36156-665c-490a-8c32-520cd1b7828a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), with building community in mind.
* Offer support, faster permitting, etc. to housing developments that build out larger shared amenities and services.

I'm not pollyannaish here; [WeWork's long-abandoned co-living spaces](https://substack.com/redirect/ddaf4f70-3bca-41e4-b69c-90c6abf65d2e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) didn't fix American loneliness. Having a shared kitchen or park doesn't automatically create community.
But design choices matter in housing: just look at how disastrous [Pruitt-Igoe](https://substack.com/redirect/9fa9a14c-09bd-4456-9b10-3f4f6a9d62fe?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) was in St. Louis, or how successful the [Fuggerei](https://substack.com/redirect/3a4b3fcf-b52b-4435-afa6-1ef250dd08c6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) has been in Germany for centuries. There's [surprisingly robust research](https://substack.com/redirect/5a0431bd-3b62-46fa-983e-26fd95ab4ee0?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) on the design choices that encourage socialization and reduce loneliness, namely around how common spaces are designed and the ways in which people are encouraged to cross paths.
People are spending less time with their neighbors, as I mentioned, and while not every neighbor is worth spending time with,16 it's a fairly logical group from which to build community.
### Policy helps, but the largest issues are cultural
Even if all of this is implemented overnight, it won't fix our loneliness crisis. It'd help, but so much of what drives loneliness is cultural. Policy solutions only get you so far.
We should push for all of these changes and dozens of other good ideas that'd help address loneliness. But the best thing any of us can do is simple: **be a good friend**.
Stay in touch with people. Invite friends to meals. Get someone's phone number if you think they'd be a cool new friend. Include people in your activities.
On any given day, the best and most direct way to address loneliness is to keep a few people from having meals alone.

1
This was written back before it got taken over by people who don't believe in the basics of science and medical innovation, but I digress.
2
A lot of these things are cross-correlated: younger people are more likely to be lower income, for instance.
3
Much of that, of course, is attributable to a [long-declining marriage rate](https://substack.com/redirect/acb6b11a-a8bd-4b95-98a1-3451759e5fe9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). But [people who have no partner](https://substack.com/redirect/3590d7ed-ae76-4f98-873e-c204d6fa28ca?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) are three times likelier to say that they're lonely compared to someone who's married, so the two aren't unrelated.
4
To be precise: it's fallen from 38% who socialize every day to 30%. There's a weird percentage-of-a-percentage thing going on with this data, so it'd be fair to say either "fallen by more than 20%" or "fallen 8%," but I felt the former was the more accurate way to put it. But I also wanted to make sure I'm being explicit with what I'm talking about.
Here's their [definition of socializing](https://substack.com/redirect/b9396a18-3f02-42af-a63c-b8a08e15e7f6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg): "Socializing and communicating includes face-to-face social communication and hosting or attending social functions."
5
Once again, this is a percentage of a percentage. [Here's the exact data](https://substack.com/redirect/461ea054-d74c-4720-8db4-193dff6555ed?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg):
> Americans are spending less time with their neighbors than they once did. From 1974 to 2018, the share of adults who reported spending an evening with a neighbor at least several times a month dropped from 44 percent to 29 percent.
I also couldn't find (reliable) post-pandemic data on neighborliness, but I have to imagine that this has accelerated since then.
6
Interestingly, the number of people who [say that they have a best friend at work](https://substack.com/redirect/2657ee28-61e4-48c7-bd4d-b5c8906758c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) is flat or even modestly trending up, though I think that's picking up the people who were less inclined to be lonely in the first place. Nonetheless, a promising counter-trend to everything else that we're seeing.
7
This particular research looked at Singaporeans and was funded by their government, but no matter how you slice it, the data on this is tragically robust. Studies come to different conclusions on the exact numbers, but there's clearly a scientific consensus that loneliness increases mortality.
8
That's true, by the way, for much of the world. [Japan has a task force](https://substack.com/redirect/c94fc726-7c58-44fa-9d79-d8cfa7d9c658?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) focused on this, for instance, but I have a few comments on their work:
* "Office for the Advancement of Measures to Address Loneliness and Isolation" is a bit of an unwieldy name.
* Man, is this one busy PowerPoint presentation.
* "Implementation of 'Loneliness and Isolation Prevention Month' campaign" is not the sort of concrete plan I was hoping for, but hey, you've got to start somewhere.

9
A lot of what the federal government focuses on is [loneliness among seniors](https://substack.com/redirect/b75fc5f1-fbc2-4416-bdb6-4b2ecc32b52c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). That's obviously important. But based on the rates of loneliness, they're actually some of the best-connected and least lonely people in this country, and I'd like to see more emphasis on addressing loneliness among younger people. This ties into an earlier topic I've written about:
[](https://substack.com/redirect/5dcaa148-4977-4c20-b110-d1ee7f624485?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)| | |

10
Examples in [Massachusetts](https://substack.com/redirect/7339ee07-0331-4336-adc7-fb931a51e22c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), [South Carolina](https://substack.com/redirect/0715c3ff-c53a-47b3-9451-587ed038c160?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), and [Wisconsin](https://substack.com/redirect/897cf68e-d201-4d53-948b-39743be350f8?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), though there are lots of others.
11
Examples in [Clackamas County, Oregon](https://substack.com/redirect/723c0c71-3164-48bf-a88d-489eeee822d9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), [San Mateo County, California](https://substack.com/redirect/d24fe880-3f55-4d1c-b3e2-64a788bc7ab3?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), and [Oakland County, Michigan](https://substack.com/redirect/ad1fadcd-fb9b-4f84-9693-81472af54be1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), though there are lots of others.
12
Some of that has to do with [rising costs associated with youth sports](https://substack.com/redirect/ca87c278-d8ac-4546-9de0-4491f2f993c1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
13
I'm also biased: some of my close friends are people I met playing Little League baseball.
14
There are a bunch of reasons for that, one of which is the decades-long decline in [rates of churchgoing](https://substack.com/redirect/39794363-57e2-4259-ab69-cef1b3332e47?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). People would often volunteer at events organized by, or at, their religious congregation.
15
This was [part of Pete Buttigieg's platform](https://substack.com/redirect/761d1ede-e88a-482e-8654-b13f2150ec5c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) when he ran for president in 2020, but I haven't otherwise seen it discussed enough.
16
I don't need research here. I'll let everyone draw from their own personal experiences on this one.

Policymakers aren't doing enough. | | | Aug 25 | | | | | | | | | | It's well understood that loneliness is a crisis in this country. The CDC notes that and references the loneliness epidemic in the U.S. and around the world. By now, everyone seems to get that. The issue is that there isn't one easy fix. The causes of loneliness are global, but the solutions are manifold, local, disjointed, and often pretty ordinary. Policymakers at every level of government aren't doing enough. ? Article summary: Americans, particularly men and younger people, are lonelier than they 've ever been. Loneliness isn 't just an individual problem. Systemic loneliness means higher mortality rates and lower workforce productivity. We need policy solutions to chip away at systemic loneliness: addressing social media use, community engagement, and housing are all part of the answer. The scale of loneliness is staggering Certainly, people feel lonelier, and both men and women say they have fewer close friends than in the past. That's especially true among men. In 1990, 55% of men said that they had six or more close friends; in 2021, , at the same time that the percentage of men who said they have no close friends increased by 5×. The same is true of young people generally: to say that they're serially lonely relative to people who are 65+. Lower-income Americans than wealthier ones.2 But this goes beyond how people are feeling. We can measure clear changes in societal norms and habits too: People are far likelier to live alone today than they were 50 years ago. versus 19% who lived alone in 1974.3 From 2015 to 2025, the number of people who socialize every day and the average time people spend socializing per day dropped at a similar rate. 26% of Americans , a 50% increase from 2003. Even before the COVID-19 pandemic, the was in steep decline, having fallen 34% between 1974 and 2018.5 As a society, we're still living in the shadow of the pandemic. I don't know if this is the primary way we're living in that shadow: that may be students having fallen behind in school, or the intense polarization of society that the pandemic exacerbated. But it's clearly one of the durable consequences. COVID didn't create loneliness; all of the data suggests it had been trending that way for decades. But it very obviously made things worse. Loneliness is a public health crisis As I've written before, government's role is to . If people are serially feeling lonely, it's worth trying to fix that on its own merits. But this isn't just a question of happiness; the problems run deeper than that. This is a workforce problem. of work than non-lonely workers--more than a full work week. By that estimate, loneliness costs employers $154 billion per year. Loneliness is also associated with . On the flip side, people with close social relationships at work Loneliness is a health problem. Serial loneliness and lack of socialization . One longitudinal study found that than non-lonely people, which is staggeringly high.7 When people talk about this as a public health emergency, this is why. What can policymakers do? It's not that the U.S. doesn't recognize that this is a problem.8 At the state,10 and local levels,11 the government says it's working to address it. But much of what these government commissions conclude is that more research is needed. Obviously, the data is important, but I don't get the sense that there's enough urgency here given the scale of this problem. One challenge is that there isn't one simple policy intervention that's going to fix this. Another is that the way people socialize is guided far more by long-evolving norms than by any public policy; you can't (nor should you) pass a law that requires people to hang out with their neighbors. But that doesn't mean there isn't more we can be doing. Below are examples of policies that would start to address America's loneliness crisis. Limit social media for children Social media isn't uniformly responsible for loneliness, but it's no accident that just as social media got really big around 2010, the percentage of 12th graders who fell precipitously and loneliness . Social media is here to stay. But elected officials aren't going far enough to protect minors, and teens under 16 shouldn't be allowed to have social media accounts: | | | | | | | ---|---|--- | May 21, 2025 | This is a short- and long-term policy solution. Short-term, kids will be less lonely; long-term, they're more likely to develop the skills they need to build and maintain friendships. Invest in lasting, recurring community events More often than not, I'm writing about policy at the federal level or at the state level, usually in Missouri. This policy intervention is at the local level--which is tricky, because local mayors and city councilors wouldn't often include "addressing loneliness" in their mandate. It should be. There's data on how team sports increase connectivity and . But since 2012, the youth sports participation rate is down, That's a real problem, especially when you consider that back in 2015, , team sports and group activities were a big part of how they stayed connected to their closest friends.13 We're moving the wrong way, and I don't think it's an accident that loneliness is climbing as youth sports participation falls. This doesn't just have to be sports, by the way. Local, affordable, community-based events--team sports or otherwise--empirically help people feel less lonely and make friends. This sort of social infrastructure needs to be seen as a public good. Promote volunteering and service years I've written before about the importance of volunteering, in part because it . But the number of hours that Americans volunteer | | | | | | | ---|---|--- | February 26, 2025 | Finding outside of the military is a start.15 Growing AmeriCorps, which invests in young adults and in the United States, is one such example. These programs help with the transition from high school to adulthood, particularly for people who don't go to four-year college. These interventions are critical for the so-called , people who are neither employed nor in school. They make up 16% of 18-to-24-year-olds, a huge number when you consider that every year that they aren't working or aren't in school, they become lonelier and much less employable. We should be growing these programs with disconnected adults in mind specifically. Design housing with the goal of addressing loneliness One of the ideas I find most intriguing: changing the regulations, guidelines, and support for housing with the specific goal of promoting community. That takes a few forms, which include but aren't limited to: Change the design of housing, particularly things like student housing and , with building community in mind. Offer support, faster permitting, etc. to housing developments that build out larger shared amenities and services. I'm not pollyannaish here; didn't fix American loneliness. Having a shared kitchen or park doesn't automatically create community. But design choices matter in housing: just look at how disastrous was in St. Louis, or how successful the has been in Germany for centuries. There's on the design choices that encourage socialization and reduce loneliness, namely around how common spaces are designed and the ways in which people are encouraged to cross paths. People are spending less time with their neighbors, as I mentioned, and while not every neighbor is worth spending time with,16 it's a fairly logical group from which to build community. Policy helps, but the largest issues are cultural Even if all of this is implemented overnight, it won't fix our loneliness crisis. It'd help, but so much of what drives loneliness is cultural. Policy solutions only get you so far. We should push for all of these changes and dozens of other good ideas that'd help address loneliness. But the best thing any of us can do is simple: be a good friend. Stay in touch with people. Invite friends to meals. Get someone's phone number if you think they'd be a cool new friend. Include people in your activities. On any given day, the best and most direct way to address loneliness is to keep a few people from having meals alone. ? But are three times likelier to say that they're lonely compared to someone who's married, so the two aren't unrelated. 4 To be precise: it's fallen from 38% who socialize every day to 30%. There's a weird percentage-of-a-percentage thing going on with this data, so it'd be fair to say either "fallen by more than 20%" or "fallen 8%," but I felt the former was the more accurate way to put it. But I also wanted to make sure I'm being explicit with what I'm talking about. Here's their : "Socializing and communicating includes face-to-face social communication and hosting or attending social functions." 5 Once again, this is a percentage of a percentage. : Americans are spending less time with their neighbors than they once did. From 1974 to 2018, the share of adults who reported spending an evening with a neighbor at least several times a month dropped from 44 percent to 29 percent. I also couldn't find (reliable) post-pandemic data on neighborliness, but I have to imagine that this has accelerated since then. 6 Interestingly, the number of people who is flat or even modestly trending up, though I think that's picking up the people who were less inclined to be lonely in the first place. Nonetheless, a promising counter-trend to everything else that we're seeing. 7 This particular research looked at Singaporeans and was funded by their government, but no matter how you slice it, the data on this is tragically robust. Studies come to different conclusions on the exact numbers, but there's clearly a scientific consensus that loneliness increases mortality. 8 That's true, by the way, for much of the world. focused on this, for instance, but I have a few comments on their work: "Office for the Advancement of Measures to Address Loneliness and Isolation" is a bit of an unwieldy name. Man, is this one busy PowerPoint presentation. "Implementation of 'Loneliness and Isolation Prevention Month' campaign" is not the sort of concrete plan I was hoping for, but hey, you've got to start somewhere. 9 A lot of what the federal government focuses on is . That's obviously important.
